section_summary: This section consists chiefly of letters from clergy, lawyers, educators, church congregations, peace advocates, and other citizens urging the Roosevelt administration to stop American exports of aircraft, oil, scrap iron, cotton, munitions, and credit that supported Japan’s war in China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could not be invoked without a presidential finding of war, did not cover most raw materials, and was not considered prudent to invoke, while emphasizing official condemnation of bombing civilians. The section also addresses the Nine-Power Treaty, aid to belligerents in Spain, petitions and resolutions for nonparticipation or embargoes, eyewitness descriptions of the bombing of Guangzhou, and statistics on licensed arms exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: J. S. Burgess to Cordell Hull concerning American supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: J. S. Burgess, Chairman, Department of Sociology, Temple University
subfiles.about: Burgess asks whether exports to Japan can be limited without drawing the United States into war.
subfiles.summary: Burgess argues that American oil, cotton, scrap iron, munitions, and armaments are helping Japan destroy China. Citing the Harper’s article “Japan’s Partner,” he proposes quotas based on prewar trade levels and sends copies to Senators Joseph P. Guffey and James J. Davis.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to J. S. Burgess
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the legal and policy limits on restricting exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green states that the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan only after a presidential finding that a state of war existed. He explains that the law does not authorize restrictions on oil, cotton, or scrap iron and says the President has concluded that invocation would not serve American interests. The reply supplies arms-license totals and repeats Hull’s condemnation of bombing civilians and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: S. Warren Sturgis to the Department of State
subfiles.from: S. Warren Sturgis
subfiles.about: Sturgis urges immediate executive action against American exports supporting Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: Sturgis deplores the inconsistency of condemning Japanese brutality while supplying Japan with war materials. He asks whether the President or State Department can curtail oil and scrap-iron exports without waiting for Congress to reconvene.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles memorandum to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Welles requests a draft reply to his former Groton School teacher, S. Warren Sturgis.
subfiles.summary: Welles identifies Sturgis as one of his former teachers. He asks Hornbeck to prepare, for Welles’s signature, a personal reply explaining the government’s position and the pertinent facts.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to S. Warren Sturgis
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Welles explains the administration’s position on restricting exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The badly reproduced draft gives Sturgis the same Neutrality Act explanation used in other departmental replies. It states that the President has not invoked the act in the Far Eastern conflict and closes with Welles’s personal regards, enclosing the Joint Resolution and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms.

subfiles.title: Blank or illegible separator page
subfiles.about: The page contains no intelligible substantive document text.
subfiles.summary: Only stray OCR characters and page artifacts appear. It is apparently a blank verso or separator between correspondence units.

subfiles.title: Earl H. Leaf to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Earl H. Leaf
subfiles.about: Leaf thanks Hornbeck for receiving a committee and reports growing public and religious opposition to aiding Japan.
subfiles.summary: Leaf considers the committee’s Washington visit successful and welcomes Senator Pittman’s resolution and church support for discouraging airplane sales to Japan. He predicts that the State Department will receive extensive public demands to end America’s partnership in the destruction of China. He also attacks Frederick J. Libby as pro-Japanese and cites Japanese commercial and propaganda material in Libby’s office.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck reply to Earl H. Leaf
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Leaf’s letter and thanks him for the information supplied.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck expresses appreciation for Leaf’s courtesy and information. The brief reply offers no substantive comment on Leaf’s political observations.

subfiles.title: Ralph O. Wells to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Ralph O. Wells
subfiles.about: Wells argues that the Nine-Power Treaty may justify prohibiting gasoline and military supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wells welcomes Hull’s efforts to discourage airplane sales to Japan but asks why gasoline and other war supplies cannot also be prohibited. He contends that supplying materials used to destroy China’s integrity conflicts with the United States’ treaty obligation to respect that integrity.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Ralph O. Wells
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department rejects the contention that the Nine-Power Treaty authorizes an export prohibition.
subfiles.summary: Green explains that the Neutrality Act would apply to both China and Japan only after a presidential proclamation and does not authorize restrictions on commodities outside the official arms list. He states that the Nine-Power Treaty contains no provision empowering the President or Secretary of State to prohibit exports. The reply defends the decision not to invoke neutrality legislation and gives licensed-export totals for both countries.

subfiles.title: Archie L. Hirst to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Archie L. Hirst
subfiles.about: Hirst forwards a unanimously adopted Methodist resolution opposing material and financial aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hirst reports that approximately five hundred Methodist clergy and laypeople heard Ralph E. Diffendorfer discuss the Sino-Japanese conflict in Madison. He asks Roosevelt to cooperate in achieving the object of the enclosed resolution and notes copies to Wisconsin’s congressional representatives.

subfiles.title: Methodist resolution against aid to Japan
subfiles.from: Clergy and laypeople representing forty churches of the West Wisconsin Conference
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The resolution endorses a southern Methodist appeal to prevent American resources from aiding Japan’s aggression.
subfiles.summary: The Madison body approves a resolution adopted by the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, at Birmingham. It joins the demand that the President and Congress prevent governmental or private material and financial resources from assisting Japan’s war against China.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Archie L. Hirst
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to the Methodist resolution by outlining the Neutrality Act and export-license policy.
subfiles.summary: Green states that arms exports to China and Japan could be prohibited only after a presidential finding of war and that non-arms commodities lie outside the Joint Resolution. He says the President has decided that invoking the act would not serve the broad interests of the United States. Updated licensed-export figures for China and Japan are included.

subfiles.title: E. Eldredge Brewster to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: E. Eldredge Brewster
subfiles.about: Brewster asks for an embargo on essential war materials used by aggressors in China and Spain.
subfiles.summary: Brewster reports concern among his congregation that American scrap iron and oil make the United States an actual participant in Japan’s aggression. He says missionaries have found American-made material in bomb fragments in Chinese cities and condemns preaching peace while profiting from war. He seeks an assurance that the administration will act regarding bombing in both China and Spain.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to E. Eldredge Brewster
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department contrasts the existing Spanish arms embargo with the absence of legal authority for one against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green explains that the Neutrality Act covers declared interstate war or sufficiently serious civil strife and notes that Spain is the only country then subject to an American arms embargo. No presidential finding of war had been made for China and Japan, and the act did not cover oil or scrap iron. The reply defends the President’s discretion and quotes Hull’s condemnation of bombing civilians and selling bombing planes.

subfiles.title: Gerald Watkins to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Gerald Watkins
subfiles.about: Watkins asks Roosevelt to stop American war-material shipments that make the United States Japan’s partner.
subfiles.summary: Watkins cites the Harper’s article “Japan’s Partner” and argues that American supplies make Japan’s undeclared war possible. He calls the policy inconsistent with naval expansion justified by fear of Japan and urges drastic enforcement of neutrality law in the name of humanity.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Gerald Watkins
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the administration has not prohibited supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green repeats that the Neutrality Act requires a presidential finding of war and would impose an arms embargo on both China and Japan. He adds that commodities outside the official arms list cannot be prohibited and that the President has judged invocation contrary to American interests. The reply provides updated arms-license figures.

subfiles.title: Mrs. F. A. Stromsten to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Mrs. F. A. Stromsten
subfiles.about: Stromsten protests the sale of American war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although much of the handwriting is poorly legible, Stromsten argues that arms and materials manufacturers profit at the expense of Chinese lives. She asks the Department to act and requests a response explaining the government’s position.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Mrs. F. A. Stromsten
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department answers Stromsten’s protest with its standard explanation of neutrality law and policy.
subfiles.summary: Green states that only a presidential war proclamation could activate a bilateral arms embargo and that the President had decided not to invoke the Joint Resolution. He supplies licensed-export values for China and Japan. The reply also repeats Hull’s public condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Rosa Lee Cosby transmittal letter
subfiles.from: Rosa Lee Cosby, Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy
subfiles.about: Cosby forwards an Executive Committee resolution concerning aircraft and war-material exports.
subfiles.summary: Cosby sends Hull a resolution adopted by the organization’s Executive Committee. The extensive letterhead identifies national officers and local sponsors of the Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy.

subfiles.title: Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy resolution
subfiles.from: Executive Committee, Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy
subfiles.about: The resolution urges Hull to discourage and refuse licenses for exports aiding attacks on civilians in China and Spain.
subfiles.summary: The committee commends Hull for discouraging aircraft sales to Japan because of the bombing of Chinese civilians. It calls for the same policy against exports of planes, engines, oil, gasoline, scrap iron, and other war implements to Italy and Germany because of their support for attacks on the Spanish Republic. It also urges refusal of export licenses for American aircraft.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Rosa Lee Cosby
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that no presidential war finding supports an arms embargo against Japan, Italy, or Germany.
subfiles.summary: Green states that the Neutrality Act would require an arms prohibition only after the President found a state of war. Because no such finding existed for Japan, Italy, or Germany, the Department claimed no authority to prevent arms exports to them. It further notes that non-arms commodities are outside the act.

subfiles.title: Paul G. Hayes to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.about: Hayes asks for lawful executive action to end American participation in Japan’s aggression.
subfiles.summary: Hayes praises the effort to discourage bombing-plane exports but argues that Japan’s campaign depends on American military supplies. He asks whether existing neutrality legislation or another law could support a comprehensive embargo without war. He rejects profits as a justification and frames his request as a plea for nonparticipation rather than armed conflict.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department describes the statutory limits and policy reasons against an embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green repeats that an arms embargo would require a presidential finding of war and would apply to both China and Japan. He says commodities outside the official munitions list cannot be prohibited and that invoking the act would not serve the general interests of the United States. Licensed arms-export totals are provided.

subfiles.title: G. Ashton Oldham to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: G. Ashton Oldham, Bishop of Albany
subfiles.about: Oldham forwards Fred H. Lysons’s legal argument for ending arms traffic with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Oldham says he hopes a way can be found to stop an unworthy and ultimately dangerous traffic in arms. Based on conversations across social groups, he believes the great majority of Americans want the traffic stopped. He encloses Lysons’s letter for the Department’s consideration.

subfiles.title: Fred H. Lysons to G. Ashton Oldham
subfiles.from: Fred H. Lysons
subfiles.about: Lysons argues that treaty enforcement, rather than a neutrality embargo, can halt American supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lysons contends that knowingly furnishing Japan with essential supplies makes the United States a participant in the assault on China and violates the Nine-Power Treaty. Citing federal cases and the Constitution, he proposes that Roosevelt suspend shipments while investigating whether they breach treaty obligations. He also warns that a Japanese victory would increase military, naval, and economic threats and urges organized public pressure.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore reply to G. Ashton Oldham
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, Counselor
subfiles.about: Moore rejects Lysons’s interpretation of the Nine-Power Treaty and reiterates neutrality policy.
subfiles.summary: Moore states that the Nine-Power Treaty gives neither the President nor Secretary of State authority to prohibit exports to Japan. He explains that a Neutrality Act embargo would follow only from a presidential finding of war and would apply to both belligerents. The reply defends the President’s decision not to invoke the act, supplies export-license figures, returns Lysons’s letter, and encloses explanatory materials.

subfiles.title: W. Russell Bowie to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: W. Russell Bowie, Rector of Grace Church
subfiles.about: Bowie cites aircraft and aviation-fuel exports and asks how the United States can stop being Japan’s accomplice.
subfiles.summary: Bowie quotes a Foreign Policy Association bulletin describing American high-test aviation fuel and aircraft sales to Japan. The bulletin characterizes the United States as a silent partner in Japanese aggression and criticizes reliance on words alone. Bowie asks for action that would answer America’s moral conscience.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to W. Russell Bowie
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department outlines the Neutrality Act and Hull’s position on bombing aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Green explains that a presidential war finding would trigger an embargo against both China and Japan, while commodities outside the arms list could not be restricted. He says the President has judged invocation contrary to the nation’s interests and provides arms-license totals. The reply closes by restating Hull’s condemnation of bombing civilians and appeals to bombing-plane manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Paul G. Hayes covering letter forwarding a Calvary Methodist resolution
subfiles.from: Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.about: Hayes forwards a petition calling for a policy of nonparticipation in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Hayes acknowledges Green’s June 30 explanation and concedes that the President lacks adequate existing authority. He asks the government to formulate a nonparticipation policy and prepare legislation while encouraging peaceful boycotts. He argues that an embargo on war materials and financial credits would pressure Japan without worsening civilian suffering or provoking war.

subfiles.title: Calvary Methodist petition to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Members of Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church, Minneapolis
subfiles.about: The petition asks Roosevelt to use every lawful means to prevent American material and financial assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The resolution describes Japan as the aggressor and condemns attacks on undefended Chinese cities, civilians, missions, and hospitals. It alleges that American raw materials, aircraft, bombs, shells, and credits sustain Japanese operations. The signers protest profits from aggression and request effective governmental prevention of direct or indirect aid.

subfiles.title: Signatures to the Calvary Methodist petition
subfiles.from: Members of Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: The sheet records the names and addresses of the people signing the July 3 petition.
subfiles.summary: Approximately forty congregants and supporters are listed with Minneapolis-area addresses. Paul G. Hayes certifies that the copy was made from the original signatures.

subfiles.title: Department of State acknowledgment to Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges receipt of the Calvary Methodist resolution.
subfiles.summary: Green summarizes the resolution’s request that American material and financial resources not aid Japan directly or indirectly. He thanks Hayes for furnishing it and promises careful attention without offering a further policy explanation.

subfiles.title: Mary E. Woolley to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Mary E. Woolley
subfiles.about: Woolley proposes publicly identifying firms that export important war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Woolley says confidential reports from Nanjing and Guangzhou intensify the picture of horror in China. She asks whether publication of the names of firms exporting scrap iron, oil, cotton, and other materials might succeed where humanitarian appeals have failed.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Mary E. Woolley
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Woolley’s proposal but says further action is not presently feasible.
subfiles.summary: Hull says her suggestion will receive full consideration and encloses the Joint Resolution and International Traffic in Arms. He explains that scrap iron, oil, and cotton are not within the presidential arms proclamation and cannot be added under the act’s terms. While emphasizing his opposition to bombing civilians, he declines to go further at that time.

subfiles.title: Stuart Innerst to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Stuart Innerst, First United Brethren Church
subfiles.about: Innerst forwards a Guangzhou appeal and asks why neutrality law has not stopped war-supply shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Innerst reports reading the enclosed Canton Committee letter to a congregation of about two hundred people. The congregation unanimously voted to send it to Hull with an appeal for government action against war-supply exports. Innerst asks for an explanation of why the neutrality law has not produced such action.

subfiles.title: Canton Committee for Justice to China appeal
subfiles.from: A. D. Fisher and Edward H. Lockwood, Canton Committee for Justice to China
subfiles.about: The committee describes Japanese bombing casualties in Guangzhou and calls for organized pressure on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The circular recounts bombing of Guangzhou’s residential and commercial districts, with vivid examples of amputees, wounded children, dead civilians, and injured Red Cross workers. It asks recipients to convene community meetings to consider an economic boycott, defensive aid to China, and relief for Chinese victims. The committee argues that helping China defeat Japan could avert a future war and naval confrontation.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Stuart Innerst
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department explains why neutrality legislation has not stopped exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green states that without a presidential finding of war there is no authority to embargo arms to Japan alone or to both China and Japan. He defends the President’s decision not to invoke the act and supplies revised export-license totals. The letter also reiterates Hull’s condemnation of bombing civilians and appeals to aircraft manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Jessie O. Butts to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Jessie O. Butts
subfiles.about: Butts asks whether the President can embargo aircraft and other war materials going to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The first page is partly duplicated or fragmentary, but the letter clearly protests the sale of bombing planes and other military materials to Japan. Butts asks about Roosevelt’s legal power to impose an embargo and calls American opposition to bombing hypocritical while the country supplies material used against defenseless civilians.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Jessie O. Butts
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department answers Butts’s embargo question with its standard interpretation of neutrality law.
subfiles.summary: Green explains that only a presidential finding of war could trigger a Neutrality Act arms embargo and that it would apply to both China and Japan. He says the President has decided that invocation would not serve American interests and provides current license figures. The reply again cites Hull’s condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Henry Stauffer to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Henry Stauffer
subfiles.about: Stauffer criticizes nominal neutrality that in practice favors Japan and forwards material concerning T. Z. Koo.
subfiles.summary: Although the second page is badly degraded, Stauffer expresses concern about government policy in the conflict between Japan and China. He argues that the United States is effectively pro-Japanese despite widespread condemnation of Japan and refers to aircraft and bombing materials. The enclosed church bulletin records a public address by T. Z. Koo on China.

subfiles.title: First Congregational Church bulletin featuring T. Z. Koo
subfiles.from: First Congregational Church, Berkeley
subfiles.about: The bulletin announces worship services and an evening address by T. Z. Koo entitled “What of China?”
subfiles.summary: The program lists morning worship, music, a sermon by Oswald W. S. McCall, and church notices. The evening service features T. Z. Koo, presented as a distinguished Christian of China under the auspices of the Institute of International Relations meeting at Mills College. It also names church staff, musicians, childcare arrangements, broadcasts, and a Plymouth House talk by Randolph Miller.
